scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8142: Hi, since the maintenance visit to the Campus 2 access
switch, people on our two floors (the 10.5.0.x group and the 10.6.0.x group)
have been saying they can't reach their usual way out of the floor any more.
It seems to be both groups at once, which feels like more than coincidence.
The person who reported it to me said something like "one of the VLANs
probably fell off the trunk" -- no idea what that means, I'm afraid. Could
someone check whether the maintenance left something out and put it back?
Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. switch4's trunk to sshswitch carries both
  VLAN 5 and VLAN 6, and both forward: VLAN 5 hosts (PC1, PC2, dc_pc5) reach
  10.5.0.254 and VLAN 6 hosts (PC3, PC4) reach 10.6.0.254, each with 0% loss. The
  correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  trunk/VLAN-pruning fault on switch4 that is not occurring (cf.
  kath4-switch4-trunk-vlan5-down, where the VLAN 5 trunk subinterface IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- switch4's trunk dropping
VLAN 5 or VLAN 6 so hosts lose their uplink -- is NOT reproducible: both VLANs
forward over the trunk. PC1 (VLAN 5) reaches 10.5.0.254 with 0% loss and PC3
(VLAN 6) reaches 10.6.0.254 with 0% loss, confirming both VLANs traverse switch4
to sshswitch.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: switch4's trunk carries both VLANs and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the VLAN 5 and
VLAN 6 host->gateway paths, finds both working, checks that switch4's trunk
subinterfaces are up, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a pruned/dropped
VLAN -- blaming switch4's trunk to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — that users on the 10.5.0.x (VLAN 5) and 10.6.0.x (VLAN 6) groups cannot reach "their usual way out" — does not correspond to any actual fault in the network. A thorough end-to-end investigation found all components operating correctly.

The Campus 2 access switch (switch4) is properly configured: its uplink (eth0) carries 802.1Q-tagged sub-interfaces eth0.5 and eth0.6 into bridges br_vlan5 and br_vlan6 respectively, and all access ports are in their correct bridge domains. The startup script matches the live running state exactly — no change was left behind by the maintenance visit.

On the aggregation side, sshswitch has br_v5 (10.5.0.254/24) and br_v6 (10.6.0.254/24) configured as the default gateways for both VLANs. Its OSPF instance correctly advertises these prefixes and the 8.8.8.0/24 simulated internet to router17 (55.5.1.1), and in return learns full campus routing (172.16.10/20/30 via router17). Router17 confirms it has learned 10.5.0.0/24 and 10.6.0.0/24 via OSPF from sshswitch.

Live ping tests confirm complete bidirectional reachability: VLAN 5 and VLAN 6 hosts reach their gateways, each other (inter-VLAN via sshswitch), all other campus VLANs (172.16.10.5, 172.16.20.9, 172.16.30.12), and the simulated internet gateway (8.8.8.254). The "Destination Net Unreachable" responses seen during early testing targeted non-existent host IPs (10.10.0.1, 172.16.30.1), not a routing gap. The network is healthy; no corrective action is needed. The user report appears to be a false alarm or a misattribution to the maintenance window.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes switch4's trunk carries both VLAN 5 and VLAN 6 and both gateways are reachable with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent documents that switch4's trunk carries VLANs 5 and 6 (eth0.5/eth0.6) and reports live ping tests showing complete reachability to the gateways, indicating baseline connectivity with no loss.

The investigation log shows direct evidence (ping results, interface/bridge listings on sshswitch, FRR configs) demonstrating VLAN 5/6 reachability and correct routing; most key claims are grounded in the captured outputs though a couple low-level switch4 interface details are asserted rather than shown explicitly. The inferences follow logically and the checks cover the essential alternatives to justify that no fault exists.
